title: The Ahl-i-Batin
summary: The Subtle Ones, a vanished Tradition of Unity and secrecy.

claims.text: Most Batini come from Middle Eastern cultures, most often Arabic ones, and the Tradition calls itself the Subtle Ones.
The Ahl-i-Batin are still based mostly in the Middle East at their five khanates, though in recent years members have turned up in the Americas, Africa and the Far East.
Batini prize formal order: without organization, they hold, the Unity cannot be acknowledged.
Training leans on mental drills, riddles and psychic defense, with Mind magic helping to persuade and shape initiates.

title: The Five Khanates
summary: The training schools of the Subtle Ones.

claims.text: A khanate is one of five Batini training schools, each with its own course of study and its own Murshid at its head.
The khanate called the Oasis of Eternal Bliss fell into corruption and was destroyed utterly.
After that fall the Batini made the post of Qutb, who links the minds of the students and watches them for corruption.
The Ikhwan at-Tawhid in Makkah has always trained more than its share of the Tradition's assassins.

title: Ghayba, the Occultation
summary: The Batini art of vanishing from all senses.

claims.text: Ghayba means occultation: a state some extreme Batini reach in which nothing physical or magical can sense them.
Facing enemies bent on their destruction, the Batini found their best answer was to disappear, at times quite literally.
Some Batini are so far lost to Occultation that no one can ask them about the Tradition's past.

title: The Batini and Iran
summary: How the Shah's fall eased Technocratic pressure on the Subtle Ones.

claims.text: The fall of the Shah of Iran and the rule of the Ayatollah ended Technocratic control there, giving the Batini a reprieve.
Training of new Qutbs began in Isfahan in October 1979.
The Batini know the political winds in Iran are shifting and expect their reprieve to end soon.

title: Batini Magic
summary: How the Subtle Ones work their Arts.

claims.text: The Batini keep their magic as subtle as they can, so that a pointed word or a raised eyebrow can draw the response they want.
The Tradition has long studied Correspondence, and each of the five factions approaches it a little differently.
Though Batini know the Solomonic codes for binding djinn, most prefer to deal with abstract spirits, using foci such as mathematics.
The Batini spread the labyrinth as a tool of meditation, and such mazes were built in many lands.

title: The Taftani
summary: The Weavers, Persian wizards of fire and open vulgar magic.

claims.text: Most Taftani are not of Arab descent and still resent the Arab conquest of Persia.
The Weavers go where they can work magic openly: open, thinly settled lands.
The Taftani claim the flying carpets of legend, and still command sandstorms and bind djinn as their heritage.
They do not share the Traditions' idea of Ascension and instead wage the War for Asha against the Druj, the soldiers of falsehood.

title: Asha and Druj
summary: The Taftani view of truth, order and the soldiers of lies.

claims.text: Asha is Truth and right order in the Taftani view, and they also use the word for the Avatar.
Those who live by Asha are said to live very long and healthy lives.
A mage whose mind is clouded by madness or drugs cannot serve Asha, the Weavers say.

title: The Last Devil King
summary: The Weavers and the end of the Devil Kings.

claims.text: In 610 the Weavers joined, uneasily, with the armies of Mohammed to destroy Al-Malek Al-Majun Ibn Iblis, last of the Devil Kings.
Many djinn served the Devil Kings in secret, hoping to enjoy both power and revenge on humanity.

title: The Djinn
summary: Spirits of smokeless fire, older than humankind.

claims.text: The djinn hold that they were made after the elemental spirits but before humans, from smokeless fire.
Djinn are Bygones, fading from the world more slowly than most such beings.
Mages who made pacts with djinn often forgot their own side of the bargain once they had what they wanted.
In the War of Enslavement djinn were shut by the score into bottles, flasks and other vessels, and most of the rest were bound to Suleiman or other viziers.
Older djinn remember those prisons and still hold a deep grudge against humanity.
